comments.author: AlgaeNo3373
comments.body:
Depends what you mean by "same quality". The reason a WoW clone one-shot might have higher quality relative to a bespoke unique game oneshot is because it essentially copies a very coherent pre-established art direction and well-trodden game design formula where high quality assets / code / designs are well-represented in the training and plentifully available online. It's tapping into a rich vein. Same applies to a racing game clone or no man's sky clone or whatever.   
  
Something more outside the distribution is still possible but you will be closer to needing to sheperd it a bit. Not all week unless you're really wanting to polish. I reckon you can probs achieve something truly bizarre and unique in a bored afternoon at this point.

replies.author: AlgaeNo3373
replies.body:
More that you both have a challenge: it has to work in unfamiliar territory and *you* have to provide the map (rather than blizzard et al doing that part for you by proxy lol)

"in the style of no man's sky" does tremendous amounts of design work for you on behalf of Hello Games, basically. 

But writing out your unique idea requires you to actually design it a bit etc. I still don't think we undersell AI capability here. It's certianly capable, it just requires more user effort.

replies.author: heavy-minium
replies.body:
In fact, the challenge is not for the AI, but for you. You have to dump a coherent idea out of your brain since it can't read minds.

And describing behavior can get excessive very fast.  
Game designers have a well-known analogy for that issue, called the [Door problem - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Door_problem) , which is also somewhat hilarious.

comments.author: i_dont_wanna_sign_up
comments.body:
It's similar to asking AI to write stories. On first glance it looks like it can infinitely generate stories exactly to your specifications, but soon you realize it's really boring and rote.

It's the same for games. You'll be amazed that it created something that works, then quickly realize it's a shallow and boring game. To actually make it good will still take a lot of effort and good design choices.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
I think an AI could... eventually. But anyone who has actually worked with it for extended game dev knows just how far we are from such a thing. Going from pretty slice (which is still woefully inferior in even the looks department to the clone it's based on) to a full game with all the systems and polish that entails is a monumental difference. It's like going from Icarus's wings to a full blown mech suit. And it only gets more unwieldy for the AI to build the larger the game gets.

But more importantly, even if AI \*could\* get to that point. If we continue at our current pace towards that, without humanity taking the time to implement a shitload of safeguards and security/societal infrastructure in place in preparation, we are probably doomed as a species. Humans would be utterly and completely obsolete at that point and without plans to handle such a thing, or to handle all the incredible security risks it would bring (with even a single fuckup ending us), we'd have too many other problems to worry about to enjoy infinite games.

So frankly I agree. I think we're either many decades from such a point, OR we will never see it because we approached it too recklessly and one of many possible catastrophes occurred as a result.

comments.author: -Star-Walker-
comments.body:
No. AI isn’t able to do „original“ stuff on its own and don’t have a sense of „this could be fun to play“ or „this looks cool“.   
Without context you have to write your entire game (mechanics, art style, sound design☝️, …) in one prompt. When you are copping an existing game design, your AI will search the web, and „steal“ from others (that’s the controversial stuff), … there is enough already written info spread on the internet.

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
$20 is not going to get you very far, even if you could write the perfect prompt to fully describe what you want in a single turn. You’ll be waiting a very long time until the required intelligence is that cheap.

What you are seeing is people with $100 or more accounts creating gameplay demos after dozens of hours of work from their frontier level agents. Personally I suspect most of them are marketing.

You’d be better off taking your $20 to Steam and just buy a game you want to play.

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body:
it's easier to "one-shot" existing games because you could point it at a video or it has all of the gameplay mechanics and art direction already in its training set so it can draw from that. It's harder to make new games because those take more iteration time to figure out.

Even when you get exactly what you asked for, since you'd be making something new you aren't drawing from an exact reference point so the thing that it made that you asked it to won't be exactly what you wanted without additional work.
